endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Record and integrate structured feedback about content provenance from operators, users, and potentially impacted communities through the use of methods such as user research studies, focus groups, or community forums.

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether collecting user and community feedback on content provenance improves provenance design, trust, or effectiveness, and no study documents the hazard itself. The recommendation rests on a single framework endorsement from NIST AI 600-1.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard, so no certainty rating can be assigned to any outcome. The only support is one framework statement using "should" language. A framework endorsement reflects expert judgment and does not substitute for comparative evidence on whether feedback changes provenance design or user trust.

NIST AI 600-1 advises organizations to record and integrate structured feedback on content provenance from operators, users, and potentially impacted communities, naming user research, focus groups, and community forums as methods. The framework is voluntary. No supplied source ties this practice to a binding federal or state requirement.

The framework names potentially impacted communities as feedback sources, but no supplied study examines who participates in such feedback or whether their input alters provenance design. Without data, a health system cannot tell whether Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients would be represented.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare provenance designs developed with and without structured user and community feedback, measuring whether users correctly recognize AI-generated clinical content, whether their trust matches the content's actual origin, and what the feedback process costs in staff time. Studies documenting how often provenance labels fail or go unnoticed in health care settings are also absent.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems that adopt this practice would need to recruit these groups deliberately and track their participation, because nothing in the supplied evidence shows that feedback processes reach them or reflect their provenance expectations.
